TL;DR for the wall-o-knowledge below: It's not a complicated system to learn and navigate, but lots of people (LOTS) get very stubborn and refuse to accept anything that isn't exactly what they want, or exactly how they think it should be.

"Fair Use" law is only relevant in a court room. If people aren't prepared and willing to take companies like Nintendo to court to dispute their claims to derivative works, they can't expect the law to protect them. That's just how the legal system works. Laws are just words that have no influence of their own until they're supported by an order from an appropriate judge. Youtube doesn't overturn content claims based on Fair Use law. They never have. What they have done in the past and continue to do is overturn claims that are disputed if the claiming party doesn't respond to the claim within 30 days. In other words, if I posted a video featuring a game made by Nintendo and Nintendo claimed it, I can dispute that claim and if Nintendo doesn't respond to the dispute within 30 days Youtube will overturn it and I will receive the revenue from the video as though it had never been claimed by Nintendo. It doesn't matter what I put in the box describing the basis for my dispute. I could type "Nintendo eats poo" in the box and it'll still get overturned because Nintendo isn't releasing it. They're losing the claim because they're not responding.

If, however, they do respond, you're fucked. Because now you're not only using content Nintendo has registered with Youtube as being theirs, you're talking out of your ass trying to get the claim released and Youtube does not like that. That's how you get copyright strikes and most MCNs will drop you if you get even one strike while you're partnered with them. And if you've been exceptionally cheeky, Youtube can just pull the plug on your channel.

But what used to happen is some guy would post copyrighted content on his channel and that content would get claimed. He would think it was a good time to play amateur lawyer and copy/paste a bunch of paragraphs from a Fair Use document he found online "proving" the right to use the content under that law. The 30 day review deadline would lapse, the claim would be overturned, and amateur lawyer guy pumps his fist in victory before he proclaims to the entire internet that he got the claim reversed by quoting fair use law. He didn't. He filed a dispute that wasn't reviewed by the claimant in time and the claim was released. But because he got it overturned and he doesn't understand what really happened, the guide video he made explaining how to get copyright claims released gets lots of views and convinces lots of Youtubers that Fair Use law is their savior. Except for those whose disputes are refuted by the claimant, who instead complain about (and typically threaten class action lawsuits against) Youtube for their "broken" system.

I get claims for audio I've used in my videos all the time. I have a legitimate, proper license to use all of the music featured in my videos but sometimes the artists branch out and start selling their music on alternate services. So I get a license from Bob's License Shack but now Tom's Royalty Free Ranch is claiming the track because they sell licenses for it, too. So I dispute the claim, with no mention whatsoever of Fair Use law, explaining where I got the license and under what terms. Tom never responds to the dispute, and 30 days after the dispute is filed, the claim is released by Youtube.

Here's a snippet from my "Youtube Claims" e-mail folder:

3rd party claims and releases

The bottom three lines show three claims that came in all at the same time, which is normal. Most of the claims I get are on older videos that were scanned as part of Youtube's ongoing audit system. In the case of two of the videos claimed, the company that claimed them is the same as the company that I have a license from so I just have to fill out a little form on their site and they always release the claim within 24 hours. It's a nuisance, but only a nuisance. My license to use the third claim is from the same company as the first two but instead it's a different company that also sells licenses for that track that is making the claim. The last claim, on the 1st line displayed, was released after 30 days because the claimant didn't respond to the dispute. That's how the system works.

With respect to successful and well-loved Youtubers like Angry Joe and ProJared, if people are going to do this stuff for a living they need to know how these things work.
